records.exact_task: A laser enters a glass block normally and a second identical laser enters obliquely. Both slow down in glass. Explain why only one changes direction.
records.protected_work: Explain why speed and direction changes are different observables.
records.shortest_route: The boundary phase relation preserves frequency; normal incidence has zero tangential direction component, so no angular change. Oblique incidence bends toward normal in higher n.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Recognize normal versus oblique refraction

representation_translation.evidence: Connect two observations to boundary direction

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Distinguish phase/frequency continuity, speed and tangential direction

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming no bending means no change of medium or speed. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Distinguish direction from speed and wavelength using the interface normal.
records.boundary: If the second medium has identical index at the light's frequency, what changes at an ideal interface?

records.protected_work: Select refractive-index comparison instead of mass density or direction-only rules.
records.shortest_route: Speed increases (c/1.30 > c/1.50); ray bends away from the normal. Need incidence within transmission domain.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate index ordering into speed/direction

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compare n then state direction

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Deciding direction based on the material's mass density or surface angle. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Compare optical indices, label the normal and direction of travel.
records.boundary: At sufficiently large angle from n=1.50 to n=1.30, what assumption may fail?

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Trace first and second refraction, establish parallelism then offset

records.exact_task: A student says every transparent slab returns an emergent ray parallel to its incident ray even if air is on one side and water on the other. Justify or reject.
records.protected_work: Demonstrate the condition for parallel emergence and expose an exception.
records.shortest_route: Combining n_left sin i=n_slab sin r=n_right sin e; if n_left≠n_right, e generally differs from i (except normal incidence). Parallel faces alone insufficient.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Recognize two-interface Snell cancellation

representation_translation.evidence: Translate outside-media difference to angle comparison

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Combine entry and exit relations, derive equality condition

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming parallel faces alone guarantee equal external direction. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Eliminate internal sine and check outside indices and face normals.

records.exact_task: A mark 24 cm below a glass surface n=1.6 is viewed from air near normal; another observer receives a ray at θ_glass=30°. Find paraxial depth and explain how to calculate the second.
records.protected_work: Select exact or paraxial geometry based on observer angle and medium.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose paraxial estimate for near normal and exact Snell/tangent for second observer

representation_translation.evidence: Translate angle data to axial intercept

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compute near estimate, exact refracted angle, then intercept

records.exact_task: A point is 12 cm below a flat interface in a transparent medium of refractive index 4/3, with air above. Two rays reach the interface 3 cm and 9 cm horizontally from the vertical through the point. On one scaled coordinate diagram construct both actual refracted rays and backward extensions; determine their axial intercepts and decide whether they locate the same virtual point.
records.protected_work: Construct two physically consistent refracted-ray representations and compare their backward axial intercepts without assuming a universal apparent point.
records.shortest_route: Draw point (0,−12) and interface z=0. For horizontal offsets 3,9, incidence angles are arctan(x/d)=14.04° and 36.87°. Snell gives refracted angles 18.87° and 53.13°. Extend each actual refracted ray backward from its interface crossing; d′=x/tan r gives 8.78 cm and 6.75 cm. Mark both intercepts on vertical axis and distinguish solid physical rays from dashed extensions. They are unequal; a universal virtual point is not exact for these off-axis rays.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select Snell and backward ray construction

representation_translation.evidence: Build two scaled ray representations with distinct axial intercepts and arrow meanings

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Recover two incidence angles from coordinates, compute refractions, project both intercepts and compare

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Material routine trigonometric calculations for both rays

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Must extend outgoing rather than incident ray; unequal intercepts matter

records.misconception: If your saved drawing extends the incident ray instead of the emergent ray, or puts both intercepts at d/n despite different angles, compare it with the constructed geometry. Otherwise record insufficient evidence.
records.repair: Plot each actual transmitted ray using its own normal angle; back-project to the vertical axis and label its intercept separately.
records.boundary: Repeat conceptually for offsets approaching zero. What common limiting depth do the intercepts approach?

records.exact_task: A learner insists the apparent depth of a pool is exactly d/n for every viewing angle. Refute using a ray at θ_water=30° in n=4/3.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate claimed ratio into comparison with angle-dependent intercept

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Apply Snell then tangent geometry then compare exact and approximate ratios

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Routine sine, inverse sine, tangent arithmetic

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Universal apparent-depth claim fails at non-small angles

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Treating small-angle sine and tangent as identical at all angles. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Use exact Snell and tangent geometry, then take the small-angle limit.
records.boundary: What happens to the backward intercept as the transmitted ray approaches grazing?

records.exact_task: A student claims that a thin converging lens can focus onto any screen at distance D>2f from a real object if moved enough. Prove or disprove.
records.protected_work: Prove the two-position boundary and reject a false inverse inference.
records.shortest_route: For p+q=D, pq≤D²/4; pq=fD requires D≥4f. Equality only p=q. Thus 2f<D<4f impossible.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate claim D>2f into inequality

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Combine pq=fD with maximum pq and equality case

records.boundary: If an opaque mount restricts travel, can D>4f guarantee both positions are experimentally reachable?
